Blackbeard the Pirate: The Final Battle of Ocracoke Inlet. How Edward Teach terrorized the Atlantic shipping lanes, blockaded Charleston, and fought a bloody last stand against Lieutenant Robert Maynard in November 1718. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the Golden Age of Piracy.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the golden age of piracy, no name struck greater terror into the hearts of merchant sailors than Edward Teach, known to history as Blackbeard. Towering, ferocious, and possessed of brilliant theatrical instincts, Blackbeard went into battle with lighted cannon fuses tucked under his hat, smoking and spitting sparks around his wild, braided black beard. After blockading Charleston harbor with a pirate fleet and seizing royal pardons, Teach retired to the quiet shallow waters of Ocracoke Inlet, North Carolina, protected by corrupt colonial officials. But on the morning of November 22, 1718, two small Royal Navy sloops navigated the treacherous sandbars for a bloody, hand-to-hand duel to the death. George brings us the thrilling story of Blackbeard's final stand.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE DEMON OF THE ATLANTIC WAVES
In the early eighteenth century, following the conclusion of the War of the Spanish Succession, thousands of unemployed privateers and merchant seamen turned to maritime piracy in the warm waters of the Caribbean and the North American seaboard. Among them arose an English mariner named Edward Teach, whose imposing physical stature and calculating intellect elevated him to the undisputed master of sea bandits. Operating from the Bahamas, Teach captured a magnificent French slave ship named La Concorde in seventeen seventeen, refitting her with forty heavy iron cannon and rechristening her Queen Anne's Revenge. Unlike the sadistic cutthroats of popular fiction, Teach rarely shed unnecessary blood; instead, he mastered psychological warfare. Before boarding a prize, Teach plaited his long, coal-black beard into braids tied with colored ribbons, strapped six loaded flintlock pistols across his chest in custom leather holsters, and tucked slow-burning hemp cannon fuses under his brimmed tricorn hat. As he swung onto merchant decks enveloped in a cloud of sulfuric blue smoke with eyes flashing in rage, terrified crews routinely surrendered without firing a shot, convinced they were being boarded by the Devil himself. Teach commanded an aura of supernatural authority among his crew, settling disputes with an iron fist and cultivating a demonic public persona that allowed him to capture dozens of merchant vessels across the Caribbean without firing a single cannon. Teach flagship Queen Anne Revenge bristled with French and English naval cannon, capable of delivering a thunderous broadside that shattered merchant hulls and forced immediate surrender on the open sea.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BLOCKADE OF CHARLESTON
In May seventeen eighteen, Blackbeard executed the most audacious act of piracy in American colonial history: the week-long blockade of Charleston, South Carolina. Sailing into the harbor with Queen Anne's Revenge and three supporting sloops manned by over three hundred heavily armed pirates, Teach seized eight merchant vessels in rapid succession, taking prominent colonial citizens hostage, including Samuel Wragg, a member of the Governor's Council. But Blackbeard did not demand chests of Spanish gold or silver ingots; his crew was suffering from a devastating outbreak of syphilis and tropical fevers. Teach sent a ransom demand to South Carolina Governor Robert Johnson: deliver a chest of specific pharmaceuticals, mercury ointments, and medical instruments, or he would execute the hostages, burn the captured fleet, and level the city's waterfront with broadsides. For five days, terrified townspeople scrambled to comply. When the chest of medicine was delivered to his flagship, Teach released the hostages unharmed—though he stripped them of their fine silk coats and gold watches—and sailed away northward toward the Carolina barrier islands, having brought a major colonial capital to its knees without shedding a drop of blood. Samuel Wragg and his fellow hostages were locked in the dark hold of the Queen Anne Revenge for over a week, trembling as pirates drank rum on deck and threatened to hang them from the yardarm if the medical chest did not arrive from the city. The Charleston city council met in emergency session, facing the agonizing reality that South Carolina provincial militia had no naval force capable of challenging Blackbeard heavily armed pirate fleet.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SHIPWRECK AT BEAUFORT AND THE ROYAL PARDON
Recognizing that King George the First had issued a royal proclamation offering full pardons to all pirates who surrendered by late seventeen eighteen, Blackbeard executed a brilliant, ruthless retirement strategy. Sailing into Topsail Inlet—modern-day Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina—Teach deliberately grounded Queen Anne's Revenge and a secondary sloop on the treacherous outer sandbars. While his stranded crew scrambled in confusion, Blackbeard loaded all the accumulated plunder, gold dust, and supplies onto a swift, shallow-draft sloop named the Adventure, abandoned forty of his crewmen on an uninhabited sandbar, and sailed away with a handpicked cadre of twenty loyal veterans. Teach traveled directly to the North Carolina colonial capital of Bath, falling on his knees before Governor Charles Eden to take the royal oath of pardon. In exchange for generous bribes and casks of captured French sugar, Governor Eden granted Teach a full pardon, awarded him legal salvage title to the Adventure, and even officiated Blackbeard's marriage to a young local merchant's daughter, establishing the retired pirate as a respected member of colonial society. Historians believe Teach intentionally scuttled Queen Anne Revenge at Beaufort Inlet to downsize his pirate fleet, break up his large and rebellious crew, and escape with the lion share of the captured treasure under the guise of an unavoidable maritime accident. Blackbeard deliberate stranding of his flagship was a masterstroke of cold-blooded calculation, allowing him to discard dozens of unruly crew members and secure the royal pardon with a smaller, fiercely loyal gang.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PIRATE DEN AT OCRACOKE INLET
Blackbeard's retirement as a respectable planter was brief. The call of the sea and the thrill of plunder were irresistible. Within months, Teach was using Ocracoke Inlet—a remote, shifting maritime passage through the Outer Banks—as his private operational base. The geography was ideal: shallow sandbars and winding tidal channels prevented heavy Royal Navy warships from entering the sound, while lookout trees on the island offered panoramic views of Atlantic merchant lanes. Teach established a trackside encampment on the edge of the island, known to this day as Teach's Hole, hosting wild, days-long rum bacchanals with visiting pirate crews, including Charles Vane and Calico Jack Rackham. When Teach brought a captured French merchant ship into Bath, falsely claiming he had found it drifting abandoned at sea, Governor Eden and customs collector Tobias Knight illegally certified the prize and took sixty barrels of sugar as their personal cut. Despairing of justice from North Carolina's corrupt government, desperate merchants appealed to Virginia's formidable royal governor, Alexander Spotswood, begging him to intervene. Tobias Knight, the colony collector of customs and chief justice, was secretly Teach business partner, receiving bribes of fine Madeira wine and Jamaican rum in exchange for alerting the pirate king to the movements of Royal Navy patrols. Governor Eden plantation at Salmon Creek became a clearinghouse for stolen merchant cargo, where pirate gold and contraband sugar were traded freely under the protection of colonial authorities.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TRAP OF LIEUTENANT MAYNARD
Governor Spotswood acted with ruthless decisiveness. Bypassing North Carolina's jurisdiction entirely, Spotswood used his personal funds to commission two small, ungunned merchant sloops, the Jane and the Ranger, manned by sixty veteran Royal Navy sailors from HMS Pearl and HMS Lyme. Command was given to Lieutenant Robert Maynard, a fearless, thirty-four-year-old naval officer known for strict discipline and cool nerve under fire. Because the shallow waters of Ocracoke Inlet could not accommodate standard naval frigates, Maynard's sloops carried no heavy cannon; his men would have to rely entirely on small arms, cutlasses, and boarding pikes. On the evening of November twenty-first, seventeen eighteen, Maynard's sloops glided silently through the breakers of Ocracoke Inlet, dropping anchor just out of sight of Teach's encampment. Spotting the naval vessels against the sunset, Blackbeard spent the night drinking rum on the deck of the Adventure with a visiting merchant captain, declaring with reckless fatalism that he would neither give nor receive quarter. Maynard men spent the freezing November night shivering on the open decks of their unheated sloops, knowing that their small arms would have to match Blackbeard heavy naval ordnance across the shallow sandbars of the inlet. Maynard drilled his sailors in cutlass combat and pistol reloading during the voyage down Chesapeake Bay, preparing his young crews for a bloody confrontation against the most feared pirate crew on the Atlantic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BLOODY CLASH AT TEACH'S HOLE
At dawn on November twenty-second, Maynard hoisted the Union Jack and ordered his rowers forward through the morning fog. Blackbeard cut his anchor cable, raised his black flag, and opened fire with nine deck guns loaded with bag shot, lead slugs, and broken glass. The devastating broadside tore through Maynard's sloops, killing the commander of the Ranger and leaving twenty-one navy sailors dead or wounded. Seeing the Jane drifting sluggishly, Blackbeard believed the battle was won. Maynard had executed a brilliant tactical ruse: he ordered all surviving sailors below deck into the hold with cocked pistols and drawn cutlasses, leaving only himself and the helmsman visible on deck. As the Adventure ran alongside and Blackbeard hurled handmade grenade flasks onto the boards, the pirate captain leaped onto the Jane's deck shouting, 'The day is ours!' Instantly, Maynard signaled his men: thirty British sailors burst from the hatches like a tidal wave, engulfing the pirates in savage, hand-to-hand combat amidst smoke and screams. The smoke was so dense that sailors fought blind, swinging cutlasses by instinct and firing pistols into the dark as the two sloops rolled against each other in the shallow breakers of the inlet. The naval sailors held their fire until the pirates were within point-blank range, unleashing a devastating volley of musket balls that threw Blackbeard boarding party into sudden shock and disarray.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE FALL OF THE GIANT
The climax of the battle was an epic personal duel between Maynard and Blackbeard. The two commanders faced each other across the bloody deck, firing their flintlock pistols simultaneously at point-blank range. Maynard's ball struck Teach in the torso, but the enraged pirate barely flinched, charging forward with a heavy cutlass. Teach shattered Maynard's naval sword with a ferocious downward blow, and was raising his blade for the killing stroke when a Scottish sailor stepped from behind and slashed Teach across the throat. Even as blood gushed from his neck, Blackbeard fought on like a wounded lion, cocking a fresh pistol until he collapsed lifeless onto the wooden planks. An autopsy revealed that Teach had sustained no fewer than twenty-five cutlass wounds and five gunshot balls before finally succumbing. Maynard severed Blackbeard's head and hung it from the bowsprit of the Jane as a gruesome trophy, dumping the headless torso into the waters of Ocracoke Inlet, where local legend whispers that the headless body swam three times around the ship before sinking into the deep. Blackbeard's death marked the sunset of the Golden Age of Piracy, cementing his status as the immortal demon of the high seas. Maynard sailed into the James River with Blackbeard severed head hanging from the bowsprit, where it remained for weeks as a grim warning to all who dared raise the black flag against the King peace on the Atlantic waters. The skull of Edward Teach was later fashioned into a silver-rimmed punch bowl according to Virginia legend, an enduring artifact of the day the British navy reclaimed the Atlantic waters from pirate rule.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Blackbeard's roar was silenced at Ocracoke, but his legend remains an eternal symbol of maritime rebellion and high-seas daring. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we feel the earth shake in South Carolina for the catastrophic Great Charleston Earthquake of 1886.
